description: We're a team of 4 from Lausanne working on the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. We're building a tool that compares landing sites and time windows near the lunar south pole, based on terrain safety, sunlight and visibility of Earth. Our team is complete. Thanks for stopping by!
summary:
CLPS Lunar Mission Browser lets planners, educators and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. For any site and moment it shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the real horizon, built from NASA LRO laser-altimeter (LOLA) terrain, and turns that into power and direct-to-Earth communication windows: sunlight and Earth-in-view percentages, time before sunset or Earth-set, and the longest night and blackout.

We built an interactive 3D Moon with live shadows, a timeline and animation, side-by-side comparison of up to eight of 26 preset sites (or custom coordinates), and a "best landing day" view. Comparisons come with reasons, not just scores. Simple mode serves newcomers; Advanced adds graphs, tables, exports, a REST API and a command line. Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.007°.

It matters because small schedule changes have large effects near the pole: in our demo, a one-week slip at one site drops power-plus-link time from 99% to 29%. The tool shows geometry, not a guarantee, and says so.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
CLPS Lunar Mission Browser answers one question for any landing spot on the Moon and any date: will a lander have sunlight and a direct line of sight to Earth? It works out where the Sun and Earth are in the sky of that spot and checks whether hills and crater walls block them, using the real shape of the ground measured by NASA’s LOLA laser altimeter. It tells you how long the Sun is up, how long Earth is in view, how long you have both together (“power + link”), and the longest night and the longest break in contact.

HOW IT WORKS
Sun and Earth positions come from the Astronomy Engine library and match NASA’s JPL Horizons service to within 0.007° (848 positions, 13 sites). For each spot, the tool traces the horizon in every direction over 600 km of real lunar ground. In 3D, shadows and Earth visibility are computed live by the graphics card. 37 automated tests run on every change.

WHAT YOU CAN DO
Turn an interactive Moon with a timeline, compare sites or dates with the reasons behind every difference, find the best landing day, or delay a landing by a week and see what changes. Simple mode is made for newcomers. Advanced mode adds graphs, exports, an API and a command line.

Interesting features

  1. Whole Moon: Whole Moon view: the lunar sites we can compare, with real LOLA relief inside the circled zones.
  2. Best site: “Best site” points straight at the best place to land for the chosen dates.
  3. Built-in assistant: Built-in help assistant: it answers questions about the tool offline
  4. Two modes. Simple mode gives quick answers for beginners. Advanced mode shows the full timelines and numbers for experts.
  5. Guided demo. A 30-second tour and a click-to-explain help mode teach a first-time user how to read the tool.
  6. Your own site. Right-click the Moon, enter coordinates, and compare your own site with the predefined ones.
  7. Compare and plan. Compare sites or dates side by side, and get the best landing days for each site.
  8. English and French
  9. Works on phones, tablets and laptops. The layout adapts down to a narrow phone screen.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
Mission planners get answers in a few clicks instead of hours. Teachers and the public get a clear, visual explanation of why the Moon’s south pole is hard. In our demo, a one-week delay at one site cuts the time with power and a link from 99% to 29%. The tool shows geometry, not a guarantee, and says so.

TOOLS
JavaScript, WebGL (three.js), Node.js, Python (NumPy, SciPy), Docker, GitHub Actions, and Claude Code (Anthropic) as an AI assistant, as described in AI_DISCLOSURE.md.

WHAT IS CREATIVE
One tool for two very different audiences: plain-language answers and a guided demo for the curious, graphs, exports and an API for the engineer. Every number comes with a reason, and the circled zones on the globe show honestly where real NASA relief data is used and where it is not yet.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED
Our team of four built this for both amateurs and professionals: a tool that would have inspired us when we were young and still helps an engineer now. We are clear about the limits: simpler horizons outside the polar region, no air on the Moon, and sunlight is not power.

NASA LRO LOLA global elevation model LDEM_64 (horizons outside the pole, relief on the globe)
NASA LRO LOLA data archive (PDS Geosciences Node)
NASA JPL Horizons (validation of Sun and Earth positions)
NASA NSSDC lunar landing sites (Apollo and other site coordinates)
NASA LRO Camera, LROC (confirmed lander positions)
NASA Deep Space Network (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra for the direct-to-Earth link)
projectRefs: Astronomy Engine (Sun, Earth and Moon positions, MIT license)
Peña-Asensio et al., published high-illumination points (arXiv:2406.19863)
USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (feature names and positions)
Wikipedia, Peak of eternal light (published coordinates and context)
